9.9a — Encryption: Keys, TLS & Public Key

When you pushed to GitHub, the URL said https — and your repo crossed the public internet unread by every router along the way. Today: how a secret can cross an open network twice, why two keys are better than one, and the one math fact protecting everything you own.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Symmetric — one shared key. The Caesar cipher you probably did in elementary school: shift letters by a key (3: CAT → FDW). Same key encrypts and decrypts. Fast, simple, and cursed by one problem: to agree on the key, you must already have a secure channel. The internet never had one.

Asymmetric — two keys, a public pair. In the 1970s, math (huge prime numbers) delivered the miracle: you publish a PUBLIC key anyone can use to lock messages to you, and keep a PRIVATE key that is the only thing that unlocks them. Publishing the lock does not reveal the key — that is the fact everything rides on. RSA: factoring a number with two 600-digit prime factors would take the world's computers longer than your lifetime; the exam wants the IDEA, not the factoring.

Symmetric (AES)Asymmetric (RSA)
KeysOne shared secretPublic + private pair
SpeedVery fastSlow
Perfect atBulk data — encrypting the actual packetsProving identity — the handshake

TLS — the handshake (https). The web uses BOTH: asymmetric to establish trust, symmetric for the actual conversation. When you see the lock icon:

1. Browser → github.com:  "hello"
2. Server → browser:    certificate + its PUBLIC key
3. Browser checks the certificate against trusted authorities
4. Browser generates a random SESSION key, encrypts it with the
   server's public key, sends it
5. Server decrypts it with its private key — the ONLY one who can
6. Both switch to fast symmetric encryption with the shared key

Step 3 is what "certificate" means — a third party vouches that this public key really belongs to github.com. Without it, anyone on your wifi could impersonate the site and hand you THEIR key (a man-in-the-middle attack).

Socratic

Why does TLS not simply use asymmetric encryption for everything (hint: your 2 MB project push at RSA speed)? The exam phrasing: "explain how symmetric and asymmetric encryption are EACH used in secure transactions" — write the one-sentence version now.

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — caesar by hand. Encrypt "BOSS" with key 3 on paper (ERVV). Pass to a partner who decrypts. Then: which letter appeared twice in the ciphertext — and why does that PATTERN (frequency analysis) break Caesar without knowing the key at all? Weak ciphers die to the STATISTICS of language, not to brute force.

Step 2 — see your own TLS. In a browser: open github.com, click the padlock → view certificate. Read the fields: issuer (a trusted authority), public key info, valid dates, and the subject (github.com). This document is Step 3 of the handshake, sitting still. Now try https://your-teacher-does-not-own-this-site.example or any bad cert page and READ the browser's refusal — you now know exactly which step failed.

Step 3 — your git connection. git remote -v in your project. Is it an https or an ssh URL? Both are encrypted. SSH is the asymmetric idea with a different protocol: your ssh keypair IS your public/private pair (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub vs the private file). If you set up GitHub Desktop, it did https + TLS. Either way, your pushes have been unread to every router (9.8a) since day one.

Bug Hunt: Crypto failures

  1. You encrypt your save file with the key stored IN the game the players download. What did you actually build (obfuscation, not security) — and why does every "DRM cracked" headline follow from this exact design?
  2. The exam classic: a site uses the same key for public and private. What breaks FIRST — and why is "key distribution" the sentence that answers it?
  3. Your password vault uses one hash for every user's same password "password123." Why does a SALT (a random per-user value mixed in) change the stolen-database story completely?
  4. Quantum computing question the exam is probing at: if factoring becomes fast, what specifically dies (asymmetric) and what survives (symmetric) — and why is the industry switching standards NOW rather than later?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Threat modeling

  1. Threat-model your game: a hypothetical cloud leaderboard. What is the asset (scores), who are the attackers (cheaters), and which trust boundary must the server own (9.8a tinker answer, upgraded)?
  2. Write the exam answer: "Which is true about public key encryption?" — make up the two wrong options too (the exam is written by people who write wrong options; knowing WHY they are wrong is the skill).
  3. Hard: why can you not reverse a HASH (one-way function), and why does your password log in as a HASH comparison rather than a decryption? (Nothing was ever encrypted — it was fingerprinted.)

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain symmetric vs asymmetric with a use case for each
  • Narrate the TLS handshake's six steps and where certificates fit
  • Read a real certificate and name what its fields prove
  • Explain why hashing is not encryption, and what a salt buys
